notes.front: What is data in use?
notes.back: Data during viewing, modifying, or synchronising between devices.
notes.explanation: It is one phase of the data lifecycle, beside data at rest on a device and data in transit between systems.
notes.example: Like a report open on screen while someone edits it, rather than filed away or in the post.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-209, Security Guidelines for Storage Infrastructure, §2.11 “Storage and Data Management”, PDF p. 24
notes.evidence: Data at rest/at the endpoint – on a server or client device. Data in transit – between storage devices, client to server, or server to server. Data in use – during viewing, modifying, or synchronizing between devices.

notes.front: What is membership inference?
notes.back: An attack whose goal is to determine whether a particular record or data sample was part of a model’s training dataset.
notes.explanation: The idea was first studied on statistical computations over genomic data, under the name tracing attacks.
notes.example: Like working out, from a published survey summary alone, whether a named person took part.
notes.source: NIST AI 100-2 E2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations, §2.4.2 “Membership Inference”, PDF p. 42
notes.evidence: In membership inference, the attacker’s goal is to determine whether a particular record or data sample was part of the training dataset used for the statistical or ML algorithm. These attacks were introduced by Homer et al. [162] for statistical computations on genomic data under the name tracing attacks.

notes.front: What is an evasion attack on a machine learning model?
notes.back: A deployment-time attack that modifies input samples into adversarial examples the model misclassifies, often imperceptibly to humans.
notes.explanation: It is one way to cause an integrity violation; poisoning at training time is the other.
notes.example: Like altering a few pixels of a scanned form so an automatic reader misreads one field while people see nothing odd.
notes.source: NIST AI 100-2 E2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations, §2.1.2 “Attacker Goals and Objectives”, PDF p. 19
notes.evidence: An attacker can cause an integrity violation by mounting an evasion attack at deployment time or a poisoning attack at training time. Evasion attacks require the modification of testing samples to create adversarial examples that are misclassified by the model while often remaining stealthy and imperceptible to humans

notes.front: What is model extraction?
notes.back: A model privacy attack in which attackers aim to extract information about the machine learning model itself.
notes.explanation: Its target is the model, not the data the model was trained on.
notes.example: Like a rival working out the settings of your prize-winning machine without ever seeing its plans.
notes.source: NIST AI 100-2 E2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations, §2.1.2 “Attacker Goals and Objectives”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: MODEL EXTRACTION is a model privacy attack in which attackers aim to extract information about the model [177].

notes.front: At which stage of machine learning are poisoning attacks mounted, and at which are evasion attacks?
notes.back: Poisoning at the training stage; evasion at the deployment stage, against a model already trained.
notes.explanation: In training, the attacker controls parts such as data, labels, parameters or code; after deployment, evasion changes the model’s predictions.
notes.source: NIST AI 100-2 E2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations, §2.1.1 “Stages of Learning”, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: During the training stage, the attacker might control part of the training data, their labels, the model parameters, or the code of ML algorithms, resulting in different types of poisoning attacks. During the deployment stage, the ML model is already trained, and the adversary could mount evasion attacks to create integrity violations and change the ML model’s predictions

notes.front: Which attacker capability do black-box evasion attacks and many privacy attacks use?
notes.back: Query access: submitting queries to the model and receiving its predictions, for example from a model offered as a cloud service.
notes.explanation: The attacker needs no control over training data or the model, only the ability to ask it questions.
notes.source: NIST AI 100-2 E2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations, §2.1.3 “Attacker Capabilities”, PDF p. 21
notes.evidence: The attacker might submit queries to the model and receive predictions (i.e., labels or model confidences), such as when interacting with an AI system hosted by a cloud provider as a machine learning as a service (MLaaS) offering. This capability is used by black-box evasion attacks, ENERGY-LATENCY ATTACK, and all privacy attacks

notes.front: Why can membership inference be harmful even without revealing a record’s contents?
notes.back: In some situations, knowing that someone is in the training set already has privacy implications, as in a study of rare-disease patients.
notes.explanation: Membership inference can also serve as a building block for data extraction attacks.
notes.source: NIST AI 100-2 E2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations, §2.4.2 “Membership Inference”, PDF p. 42
notes.evidence: In certain situations, determining that an individual is part of the training set already has privacy implications, such as in a medical study of patients with a rare disease. Moreover, membership inference can be used as a building block for mounting data extraction attacks

notes.front: Besides membership inference, what are two attack objectives against the privacy of training data?
notes.back: Any two of: data reconstruction, training data extraction, attribute inference, property inference.
notes.explanation: The guidance introduces these with “such as”, so the list is not closed.
notes.source: NIST AI 100-2 E2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations, §2.1.2 “Attacker Goals and Objectives”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: The attacker could have different objectives for compromising the privacy of training data, such as DATA RECONSTRUCTION [110] (inferring the content or features of training data), MEMBERSHIP-INFERENCE ATTACK [162, 343] (inferring the presence of data in the training set), TRAINING DATA EXTRACTION [59, 63] (extracting training data from generative models), ATTRIBUTE INFERENCE ATTACKS [184, 409]

notes.front: Why does adversarial machine learning count model extraction as a privacy attack?
notes.back: Its term “privacy” covers attacks on a model’s confidentiality, such as extracting its weights or architecture, as well as exposure of training data.
notes.explanation: The field says “privacy” where traditional security taxonomies say “confidentiality”, so taking information about the model itself falls under it.
notes.source: NIST AI 100-2 E2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations, §2.1.2 “Attacker Goals and Objectives”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: the AML field has tended to use the top-level term “privacy” to encompass both attacks against the confidentiality of a model (e.g., those that extract information about a model’s weights or architecture) and those that cause violations of expected privacy properties of model outputs (e.g. by exposing model training data)

notes.front: Can model extraction produce an exact copy of a machine learning model?
notes.back: Exact extraction has been shown impossible; a functionally equivalent model with similar performance can be reconstructed.
notes.explanation: Researchers have also shown that even extracting a functionally equivalent model is computationally prohibitive.
notes.source: NIST AI 100-2 E2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations, §2.4.4 “Model Extraction”, PDF p. 44
notes.evidence: However, Jagielski et al. [177] have shown the exact extraction of ML models to be impossible. Instead, a functionally equivalent model can be reconstructed that is different than the original model but achieves similar performance at the prediction task. Jagielski et al. [177] have shown that even the weaker task of extracting functionally equivalent models is computationally prohibitive (NP-hard).

notes.front: What new kinds of dependency does AI development add to the software supply chain?
notes.back: Among others: data collection and scoring, third-party AI models, and third-party plugins.
notes.explanation: Since AI is software, it also inherits traditional supply chain weaknesses such as reliance on third-party dependencies.
notes.source: NIST AI 100-2 E2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations, §3.2 “Supply Chain Attacks and Mitigations”, PDF p. 54
notes.evidence: Since AI is software, it inherits many of the vulnerabilities of the traditional software supply chain, such as reliance on third-party dependencies. AI development also introduces new types of dependencies, including data collection and scoring, the integration or adaptation of third-party-developed AI models, and the integration of third-party-developed plugins into AI systems.

notes.front: What does mitigating AI supply chain risk require?
notes.back: A multifaceted approach: existing software supply chain risk practices plus management of AI-specific risks, for example through provenance information.
notes.explanation: Provenance information is applied to the additional artefacts that AI brings into the supply chain.
notes.source: NIST AI 100-2 E2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations, §3.2 “Supply Chain Attacks and Mitigations”, PDF p. 54
notes.evidence: Mitigating the security challenges in AI supply chain management is complex and requires a multifaceted approach that combines existing practices for software supply chain risk management with the management of AI-specific supply chain risks, such as through the use of provenance information for the additional artifacts involved [159, 267].

notes.front: How can attackers exploit developers’ use of third-party foundation models?
notes.back: By offering maliciously designed models, such as pre-trained models that enable backdoor or targeted poisoning attacks.
notes.explanation: The attack arrives through the supply chain: the poison comes with the supplied model.
notes.source: NIST AI 100-2 E2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations, §3.2.2 “Model Poisoning Attacks”, PDF p. 55
notes.evidence: In GenAI, it is common for developers to use foundation models developed by third parties. Attackers can take advantage of this fact by offering maliciously designed models, such as pre-trained models that enable a BACKDOOR POISONING ATTACK or TARGETED POISONING ATTACK.

notes.front: Why do attacks such as prompt injection create extra risk when a model runs as an agent?
notes.back: Agents can take actions using tools, so attackers may hijack them to execute arbitrary code or exfiltrate data from their environment.
notes.explanation: The danger comes from the tools: an agent that can act can be made to act for the attacker.
notes.source: NIST AI 100-2 E2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations, §3.5 “Security of Agents”, PDF p. 67
notes.evidence: However, because agents can take actions using tools, these attacks can create additional risks in this context, such as enabling actors to hijack agents to execute arbitrary code or exfiltrate data from the environment in which they are operating.

notes.front: Assuming prompt injection is possible whenever a model sees untrusted input, what are two design approaches to contain it?
notes.back: Using multiple models with different permissions; letting models reach untrustworthy data sources only through well-defined interfaces.
notes.explanation: Both designs start from the assumption that injection will happen, and limit what an injected model can reach.
notes.source: NIST AI 100-2 E2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations, §3.4 “Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks and Mitigations”, PDF p. 67
notes.evidence: with the assumption that prompt injection attacks are possible if a model is exposed to untrusted input sources, such as by using multiple LLMs with different permissions [145, 405] or by allowing models to interact with potentially untrustworthy data sources only through well-defined interfaces [410].

notes.front: What does public cloud guidance say about protecting data in use with cryptography?
notes.back: It is an emerging area with little practical result to offer, leaving trust mechanisms as the main safeguard.
notes.explanation: Where cryptography cannot yet protect data while it is processed, trust has to carry the load.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-144, Guidelines on Security and Privacy in Public Cloud Computing, PDF p. 40
notes.evidence: Protecting data in use is an emerging area of cryptography with little practical results to offer, leaving trust mechanisms as the main safeguard [Gre09, Pro10].

notes.front: In the AI RMF, which function establishes the context to frame the risks related to an AI system?
notes.back: Map.
notes.explanation: Context matters because the people in charge of one part of an AI system’s lifecycle often cannot see or control the other parts.
notes.source: NIST AI 100-1, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), §5.2 “Map”, PDF p. 29
notes.evidence: The MAP function establishes the context to frame risks related to an AI system.

notes.front: In the AI RMF, which function allocates risk resources to the risks that have been mapped and measured?
notes.back: Manage.
notes.explanation: It does this regularly and as Govern defines, and its risk treatment includes plans to respond to, recover from and communicate about incidents.
notes.source: NIST AI 100-1, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), §5.4 “Manage”, PDF p. 36
notes.evidence: The MANAGE function entails allocating risk resources to mapped and measured risks on a regular basis and as defined by the GOVERN function. Risk treatment comprises plans to respond to, recover from, and communicate about incidents or events.

notes.front: A hospital publishes a disease-prediction model. A researcher queries it to learn whether a named patient’s record was used in training. What attack is this?
notes.back: Membership inference
notes.choices:
A) Evasion attack
B) Model extraction
C) Data poisoning
D) Membership inference
notes.choicesExplained: A changes inputs to fool predictions. B targets the model’s own details. C tampers with the training data.
notes.explanation: Determining whether a particular record was in the training dataset is membership inference.
notes.source: NIST AI 100-2 E2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations, §2.4.2 “Membership Inference”, PDF p. 42
notes.evidence: In membership inference, the attacker’s goal is to determine whether a particular record or data sample was part of the training dataset used for the statistical or ML algorithm.

notes.front: Fraudsters subtly alter scanned cheque images so a deployed recognition model misreads the amounts, while clerks notice nothing. What attack is this?
notes.back: Evasion attack
notes.choices:
A) Membership inference
B) Evasion attack
C) Model extraction
D) Data poisoning
notes.choicesExplained: A asks who was in the training data. C copies information about the model. D happens at training time, not on a deployed model.
notes.explanation: Modified inputs that a deployed model misclassifies, while staying imperceptible to people, are the mark of an evasion attack.
notes.source: NIST AI 100-2 E2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations, §2.1.2 “Attacker Goals and Objectives”, PDF p. 19
notes.evidence: Evasion attacks require the modification of testing samples to create adversarial examples that are misclassified by the model while often remaining stealthy and imperceptible to humans

notes.front: A competitor sends thousands of queries to a company’s paid prediction service and uses the answers to build a model that performs almost as well. What attack is this?
notes.back: Model extraction
notes.choices:
A) Model extraction
B) Membership inference
C) Evasion attack
D) Prompt injection
notes.choicesExplained: B asks whether a record was in the training data. C fools the model on particular inputs. D smuggles instructions into a generative model’s input.
notes.explanation: Rebuilding a functionally equivalent model with similar performance from queries is model extraction.
notes.source: NIST AI 100-2 E2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations, §2.4.4 “Model Extraction”, PDF p. 44
notes.evidence: Instead, a functionally equivalent model can be reconstructed that is different than the original model but achieves similar performance at the prediction task.

notes.front: Before a spam filter is retrained, an attacker slips mislabelled samples into its training data. What kind of attack is this?
notes.back: Data poisoning
notes.choices:
A) Evasion attack
B) Model extraction
C) Data poisoning
D) Membership inference
notes.choicesExplained: A works on an already-trained model at deployment. B and D extract information rather than tampering with training.
notes.explanation: Controlling part of the training data or its labels during training leads to poisoning attacks.
notes.source: NIST AI 100-2 E2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations, §2.1.1 “Stages of Learning”, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: During the training stage, the attacker might control part of the training data, their labels, the model parameters, or the code of ML algorithms, resulting in different types of poisoning attacks.

notes.front: An analyst has a customer spreadsheet open and is changing figures in it. Which data state is this?
notes.back: Data in use
notes.choices:
A) Data at rest
B) Data in transit
C) Data in use
D) Data traveling outside the security perimeter
notes.choicesExplained: A is data stored on a device. B is data moving between systems. D covers downloads or media being shipped.
notes.explanation: Data being viewed or modified is data in use.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-209, Security Guidelines for Storage Infrastructure, §2.11 “Storage and Data Management”, PDF p. 24
notes.evidence: Data in use – during viewing, modifying, or synchronizing between devices.

notes.front: A team downloads a pre-trained model from a public hub and fine-tunes it for its product. Which risk comes from this supply chain step?
notes.back: The model may have been built by its supplier to carry a backdoor
notes.choices:
A) The model may have been built by its supplier to carry a backdoor
B) The fine-tuning will leak the team’s passwords
C) The model will stop working after a set date
D) The hub will own the finished product
notes.choicesExplained: B, C and D are not risks the guidance attaches to third-party models.
notes.explanation: Attackers can offer maliciously designed pre-trained models that enable backdoor or targeted poisoning.
notes.source: NIST AI 100-2 E2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations, §3.2.2 “Model Poisoning Attacks”, PDF p. 55
notes.evidence: Attackers can take advantage of this fact by offering maliciously designed models, such as pre-trained models that enable a BACKDOOR POISONING ATTACK or TARGETED POISONING ATTACK.

notes.front: An applicant crafts inputs that make a loan-approval model approve his applications against the lender’s rules. Which attacker objective does this serve?
notes.back: Integrity violation
notes.choices:
A) Availability breakdown
B) Privacy compromise
C) Data portability
D) Integrity violation
notes.choicesExplained: A would deny the service to others. B would leak data or model details. C is not an attacker objective at all.
notes.explanation: Forcing the model to misperform against its intended objectives, in the adversary’s favour, is an integrity violation.
notes.source: NIST AI 100-2 E2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations, §2.1.2 “Attacker Goals and Objectives”, PDF p. 19
notes.evidence: An INTEGRITY VIOLATION attack is a deliberate interference with a PredAI system to force it to misperform against its intended objectives and produce predictions that align with the adversary’s objective.

notes.front: A company deploys an AI agent that reads customer emails and can call internal tools. Which design best limits the damage if an email carries injected instructions?
notes.back: Separate models with different permissions, and untrusted content reached only through well-defined interfaces
notes.choices:
A) Give the agent administrator rights so it never fails
B) Separate models with different permissions, and untrusted content reached only through well-defined interfaces
C) Turn off the agent’s logs to save storage
D) Let the agent install any tool it asks for
notes.choicesExplained: A and D widen what a hijacked agent could do. C removes evidence without reducing risk.
notes.explanation: Designs that assume injection will happen use models with different permissions and well-defined interfaces to untrusted data.
notes.source: NIST AI 100-2 E2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations, §3.4 “Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks and Mitigations”, PDF p. 67
notes.evidence: such as by using multiple LLMs with different permissions [145, 405] or by allowing models to interact with potentially untrustworthy data sources only through well-defined interfaces [410].
